context_blurb:
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, but its energy was made deep inside the Sun, in a core some fifteen million degrees Celsius hot. By weighing atoms, catching ghostly particles and counting dark spots, astronomers have learned how the Sun shines and how old it is.

For ages the Sun looked like a great fire. In 1862 Lord Kelvin worked out that even the best chemical fuel could give only about three thousand years of the Sun's heat, so a burning Sun would have burned out in a few thousand years, too soon for Earth's long history. Its stored heat and slow shrinking could keep it shining only some tens of millions of years.

In Cambridge, Francis Aston found that a helium atom is a little lighter than four hydrogen atoms put together, by about one part in 120. In 1920, at Cardiff, Arthur Eddington argued that shrinking could never power the stars for so long, so they must shine by building helium out of hydrogen. The lost mass comes out as energy, while breaking helium apart would cost energy instead.

That fusion happens only in the core, and slowly: at the very centre, models give under three hundred watts for each cubic metre, roughly the heat a compost heap makes. The Sun blazes anyway because its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing, and those small outputs add up.

The energy escapes slowly, because the gas around the core is so dense that light travels only a tiny way before an atom soaks it up and sends it off again in a random direction, so it zigzags outward like a lost walker. Rising and sinking gas then carries the heat through the outer third far faster.

Fusion also makes neutrinos, tiny particles that cross the whole Sun in about two seconds. From the late 1960s Ray Davis caught them in a huge tank of chlorine-rich cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota gold mine, but found only a third of the number that solar models predicted. Chlorine reacts with just one of the three kinds of neutrino. In 2001 and 2002, Canada's Sudbury Neutrino Observatory counted all three kinds at once: the total matched the models, but only a third were of Davis's kind. Nothing had gone missing, because neutrinos change kind on their way from the core, which they can do only if they have mass.

The Sun's age, about 4.6 billion years, comes from dating the Solar System's first solids, grains rich in calcium and aluminium kept in some meteorites, by the radioactive elements inside them. Earth's oldest rocks are younger, about four billion years, because most of its first crust has been melted and remade.

Behind a solar filter, sunspots look black, though they are thousands of degrees hot. In 1908 George Ellery Hale found strong magnetism in them from the way it split the lines in their light. That magnetism chokes off the rising and sinking gas that carries heat up from below, so a spot is 1,500 degrees or more cooler than the surface around it and glows dimmer.

From 1826 the Dessau pharmacist Heinrich Schwabe spent every clear day for seventeen years searching the Sun for an unknown planet inside Mercury's orbit, logging each sunspot. He never found his planet, but his log showed the number of spots rising and falling over about ten years. The cycle averages about eleven years, and it is magnetic: each cycle, the Sun's magnetic poles swap places.

Magnetic energy stored near sunspots can burst out as a flare. On 1 September 1859 Richard Carrington saw two dazzling patches of white light blaze up among the spots and vanish within minutes. Some seventeen hours later a cloud of magnetised gas from the Sun struck Earth, and telegraph systems on both sides of the Atlantic threw sparks. Earth's changing magnetic field drove the current, because a swinging magnetic field drives electric current along a long wire, even with the batteries unhooked.

In 1957 Fred Hoyle, William Fowler and the Burbidges, Margaret and Geoffrey, set out how stars forge heavier atoms as they shine and explode, making most of what is in your body. The great exception is the hydrogen in your water: it was made in the Big Bang, before any star shone, and it is the very fuel that stars fuse into everything heavier. The oxygen bonded to it, like your carbon, was forged in stars.
